Listing Memorandum




                               US$750,000,000 8.500% Senior Secured Notes due 2032
We are offering US$750,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 8.500% senior secured notes due 2032. The notes will mature on October 28, 2032.
Interest will accrue from October 29, 2025, and will be payable semi-annually, in arrears on April 28 and October 28 of each year, commencing on April
28, 2026.
The notes will be guaranteed on a senior basis by the subsidiary guarantors described in “Description of Notes” (the “Subsidiary Guarantors”) and secured
by first priority liens on the Collateral (as defined in “Description of Notes”). The notes will rank equal in right of payment with all other existing and future
senior indebtedness of the Company, and the guarantees will rank equal in right of payment with all other existing and future indebtedness of the Subsidiary
Guarantors. See “Description of Notes—General.” The notes and the guarantees will be senior obligations of the Company and the Subsidiary Guarantors,
respectively, secured by first priority liens on the Collateral (as defined herein), subject to permitted liens and certain other exceptions as described under
“Description of Notes—Collateral.” The notes and the guarantees will be effectively (i) pari passu with all existing and future indebtedness permitted to be
secured by a first-priority lien on the Collateral, subject to permitted collateral liens and existing liens and rights on the Collateral, (ii) senior in right of
payment to all existing and future subordinated indebtedness of the Company and the Subsidiary Guarantors, and (iii) senior to all other existing and future
senior indebtedness of the Company and the Subsidiary Guarantors that is unsecured or that is secured by junior liens or liens that are not on the Collateral,
in each case to the extent of the value of the Collateral. The notes and the guarantees will be effectively subordinated to (i) the extent of the value of the
collateral securing (x) all existing and future secured indebtedness of the Company to the extent such security interest does not also secure the notes, and (y)
all existing and future secured indebtedness of the Subsidiary Guarantors to the extent such security interest does not also secure the guarantees, (ii) all
additional existing and future indebtedness of the Company’s subsidiaries that does not provide a guarantee, and (iii) obligations of the Company or the
Subsidiary Guarantors preferred by statute or by operation of law.
We may redeem the notes in whole or in part at any time on or after October 28, 2028 at a redemption price specified in this offering memorandum, plus
accrued and unpaid interest, if any, to the date of redemption. Before October 28, 2028, we may redeem some or all of the notes at a redemption price equal
to 100% of the principal amount of the notes redeemed plus a “make-whole” premium, plus accrued and unpaid interest, in any, to the date of redemption.
Upon the occurrence of specified events relating to tax law as a result of which we will be obligated to pay additional interest amounts with respect to the
notes, the notes will be redeemable at a price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the notes, plus accrued and unpaid interest, if any, to the date of
redemption. We may also redeem up to 35% of the aggregate principal amount of the notes using the proceeds of certain equity offerings completed on or
before October 28, 2028 at the redemption price set out in this offering memorandum, plus accrued and unpaid interest, if any, to the date of redemption. If
we experience specific kinds of changes in control, or, subject to certain conditions, we sell certain of our assets, we must offer to purchase the notes. See
“Risk Factors” beginning on page 16 for a discussion of certain risks that you should consider in connection with an investment in the notes.

                                        Issue price:    100.000% plus accrued interest, if any, from October 29, 2025.


The notes have not been registered under the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”), or the securities laws of any jurisdiction.
We are offering the notes only to qualified institutional buyers under Rule 144A under the Securities Act and non-U.S. persons outside the United
States in reliance on Regulation S of the Securities Act. For a description of certain restrictions on transfer of the notes, see “Transfer
Restrictions.”
Application has been made to list the notes on the Official List of the Luxembourg Stock Exchange and to admit the notes to trading on the Euro MTF
Market of the Luxembourg Stock Exchange. Our LEI code is 549300XKJ91C4SZLG750. This offering memorandum constitutes a prospectus for the
purposes of the Luxembourg law on prospectuses for securities, dated July 16, 2019. This offering memorandum constitutes a prospectus for the purpose of
Part IV of the Luxembourg law on prospectuses for securities, dated July 16, 2019. Currently, there is no public market for the notes.
None of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, any U.S. state securities commission or any securities regulatory authority has approved or
disapproved of these securities or determined whether this offering memorandum is accurate or complete. Any representation to the contrary is a criminal
offense.
The notes and the information contained in this offering memorandum have not been, and will not be, registered with or approved by the Peruvian
Superintendency of the Securities Market (Superintendencia del Mercado de Valores, or “SMV”) or the Lima Stock Exchange (Bolsa de Valores de Lima,
or the “BVL”). Accordingly, the notes cannot be offered or sold in the Republic of Peru (“Peru”), except if such offering is considered a private offering

enacted by Supreme Decree No. 020-2023-EF, as amended, establishes, among other things, that any particular offer may qualify as private if it is directed
exclusively to institutional investors. The notes may not be offered or sold in Peru or in any other jurisdiction except in compliance with the securities laws
thereof.
Delivery of the notes was made to investors in book-entry form through The Depository Trust Company (“DTC”) for the accounts of its direct and indirect
participants, including Euroclear Bank S.A.N.V., as operator of the Euroclear System (“Euroclear”), and Clearstream Banking, société anonyme
(“Clearstream”), on October 29, 2025.

                                      NOTICE TO CERTAIN INVESTORS

Notice to Investors within the United Kingdom

     The notes are not intended to be offered, sold or otherwise made available to and should not be offered, sold or
otherwise made available to any retail investor in the United Kingdom (“UK”). For these purposes, a retail investor
means a person who is one (or more) of: (i) a retail client, as defined in point (8) of Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No
2017/565 as it forms part of domestic law by virtue of the European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 (“EUWA”); (ii) a
customer within the meaning of the provisions of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, as amended
(“FSMA”) and any rules or regulations made under the FSMA to implement Directive (EU) 2016/97, where that
customer would not qualify as a professional client, as defined in point (8) of Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) No
600/2014 as it forms part of domestic law by virtue of the EUWA; or (iii) not a qualified investor as defined in
Article 2 of Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 as it forms part of domestic law by virtue of the EUWA. Consequently no
key information document required by Regulation (EU) No 1286/2014 as it forms part of domestic law by virtue of
the EUWA (the “UK PRIIPs Regulation”) for offering or selling the notes or otherwise making them available to
retail investors in the United Kingdom has been prepared and therefore offering or selling the notes or otherwise
making them available to any retail investor in the United Kingdom may be unlawful under the UK PRIIPs
Regulation.

Notice to Investors within the European Economic Area

                                       ENFORCEMENT OF JUDGMENTS

          We are incorporated as a publicly held corporation (sociedad anónima abierta) under the laws of Peru.
Substantially all of our directors and officers, as well as certain of the experts named herein, reside in Peru or
elsewhere outside the United States and a substantial portion of their assets may be, and substantially all of our
assets are, located in Peru or elsewhere outside the United States. As a result, it may not be possible for investors to
effect service of process within the United States or elsewhere outside Peru upon us or upon any of our directors or
officers or to enforce against such parties in courts outside Peru judgments predicated solely upon the civil liability
provisions of the federal securities laws of the United States or other foreign regulations. In addition, there may be
doubt as to whether the courts of Peru would enforce in all respects, to the same extent and in as timely a manner as
a U.S. court or foreign court, an action predicated solely upon the civil liability provisions of the U.S. federal
securities laws or other foreign regulations.

          We have been advised by Payet, Rey, Cauvi, Pérez Abogados, our Peruvian counsel, that any final and
conclusive judgment for a fixed and definitive sum obtained against us and/or any of the Subsidiary Guarantors in
any foreign court having jurisdiction in respect of any suit, action or proceeding against us and/or any of the
Subsidiary Guarantors for the enforcement of any of the obligations assumed under this offering memorandum or
the notes would, upon request, be deemed valid and enforceable in Peru through an exequatur judiciary proceeding
(which does not involve the reopening of the case or reexamination of the merits of the case), provided that:
(a) there is in effect a treaty between the country where said foreign court sits and Peru regarding the recognition
and enforcement of foreign judgments; or (b) in the absence of such a treaty, the original judgment is ratified by the
Peruvian courts (Cortes de la República del Perú), provided that the following conditions and requirements are met:

         (i)      the foreign judgment does not resolve matters under the exclusive jurisdiction of
         Peruvian courts (and the matters contemplated by this offering memorandum or the notes are not
         matters under the exclusive jurisdiction of Peruvian courts);

         (ii)     the relevant foreign court had jurisdiction under its own conflicts of law rules and under
         general principles of international procedural jurisdiction;

         (iii)    the defendant was served in accordance with the laws of the place where such proceeding
         took place, was granted a reasonable opportunity to appear before such foreign court, and was
         guaranteed due process rights;

         (iv)     the foreign judgment has the status of res judicata in the jurisdiction of the court
         rendering such judgment;

         (v)      there is no pending litigation in Peru between the same parties for the same dispute,
         which shall have been initiated before the commencement of the proceeding that concluded with
         the foreign judgment;

         (vi)    the foreign judgment is not incompatible with another judgment that fulfills the
         requirements of recognition and enforceability established by Peruvian law unless such foreign
         judgment was rendered first;



                                                           iv

(vii)   the foreign judgment is not contrary to public policy (orden público) or good morals
         (buenas costumbres) of Peru;

         (viii)  it is not proven that the foreign court that rendered the foreign judgment denies
         enforcement of Peruvian judgments or engages in a review of the merits thereof;

         (ix)      a copy of such judgment has been (a) in case of jurisdictions that are party to the 1961
         Hague Convention Abolishing the Requirements of Legalization of Foreign Public Documents
         (“The Hague Apostille Convention”), duly apostilled by the competent authority of the jurisdiction
         of the issuing court, or (b) in case of jurisdictions that are not party to The Hague Apostille
         Convention, certified by Peruvian consular authorities and, in each case, is accompanied by a
         certified and officially translated copy of such judgment into Spanish by a Peruvian Certified
         translator; and

         (x)      the applicable court taxes or fees have been paid.

         We have no reason to believe that any of our obligations relating to the notes would be contrary to Peruvian
public policy (orden público), good morals (buenas costumbres) and international treaties binding upon Peru or
generally accepted principles of international law.

         Some of our properties could be subject to the exemption set forth under Article No. 616 of the Peruvian
Civil Procedure Code (Legislative Decree No. 768, whose sole unified text was approved through Ministerial
Resolution No. 10-93-JUS) pursuant to which the property of any private entity assigned to render essential public
services may not be subject to preliminary attachments (medida cautelar) that could affect the normal rendering of
such services.

          In the past, Peruvian courts have enforced judgments rendered in the United States based on legal
principles of reciprocity and comity. However, the United States does not currently have a treaty with Peru
providing for reciprocal recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters. Therefore,
unless the above-mentioned requirements are satisfied, a final judgment for payment of money rendered by a federal
or state court in the United States based on civil liability, whether or not predicated solely upon U.S. federal
securities laws, may not be enforceable, either in whole or in part, in Peru. However, if the party in whose favor
such unenforced final judgment was rendered brings a new suit in a competent court in Peru, such party may submit
to the Peruvian court the final judgment rendered in the United States. Under such circumstances, a judgment by a
federal or state court of the United States against us and/or of the Subsidiary Guarantors may be regarded by a
Peruvian court only as evidence of the outcome of the dispute to which such judgment relates, and a Peruvian court
may choose to re-hear the dispute. In addition, awards of punitive damages in actions brought in the United States or
elsewhere are unenforceable in Peru.

         This offering memorandum presents our EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA information for the convenience
of investors. EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA are presented because we deem them to better represent our operating
and economic performance, although they are not IFRS-based measures of liquidity or performance. EBITDA is
calculated as net (loss) profit for the year/period before income tax expense, financial expenses (income),
depreciation and amortization during such period. Adjusted EBITDA is calculated by eliminating from the
calculation of EBITDA: (a) any non-recurring items during such period, (b) gains or losses on the sale of property
(other than the sale of property in the ordinary course of business) during such period, (c) any other non-cash items
deducted from or included in the calculation of pre-tax net income for such period (other than items that will require

cash payments and for which an accrual or reserve has been, or is required by IFRS to be, made), and (d) foreign
exchange gains or losses upon loans and foreign currency translation adjustments or monetary correction and bank
charges. We believe that EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA, while providing useful information, should not be
considered in isolation or as a substitute for net income as an indicator of operating performance, or as an alternative
to cash flow as a measure of liquidity. Additionally, our calculation of EBITDA and Adjusted EBITDA may be
different from the calculation used by other companies and therefore, comparability may be affected.

          As used in this offering memorandum, “cash cost” is on a by-product basis, is calculated in accordance
with the methodology specified by Wood Mackenzie Limited (“Wood Mackenzie”) for determination of C1 cost
(cash cost) and includes all direct cash costs of mining, including costs associated with extraction, leaching and
further processing of metal ores, as well as labor, transportation and physical plant costs associated with those
processes, and net of income from sales of by-products. Cash cost figures are given as nominal dollar amounts,
usually expressed as dollars per metric tonne, and exclude provisions, amortization, depreciation and central office
costs and purchases of concentrates. Cash cost is presented because it is a widely used measure of costs, although it
is not an IFRS-based measure of cost. We believe that cash cost, while providing useful information, should not be
considered in isolation or as a substitute for costs of sales, costs of selling and administrative expenses, or as an
indicator of costs.

                                 MINERAL RESOURCE AND RESERVE DATA

          In this offering memorandum, we present our holdings in, or rights to, mineral deposits in two categories:
(i) resources and (ii) reserves, as is standard in the industry. Our ore reserve and mineral resource estimates are
consistent with the application of internationally used classifications. The information on reserves and resources
included in this offering memorandum has been estimated following the intent of international definitions as
established by the Joint Ore Reserves Committee Code of Australia (“JORC”). Such information has been prepared
under the general supervision of our chief geological engineer in consultation with recognized consultant geologists
and engineers, acting as competent persons. This information is not, however, typically subject to review or audit
by independent or external experts.

         Mineral resources are ore bodies of economic value that have been identified and evaluated through
exploration, reconnaissance and sampling. Resources are estimated based on geological knowledge about the



                                                          vii

deposit, which is based on scientific concepts concerning the formation of minerals such as oxides, sulfides and
mixed ores, as well as available knowledge concerning the geological continuity of the mineralized sectors. This is
based on technical parameters, such as robustness of the genetic-geological model and its validation through
drillings.

          Resources may be subdivided further, based on the degree of knowledge that we have of their extent and
composition. If our knowledge of the resources is extensive and direct, they are measured resources; if our
knowledge of them is substantial but less extensive, they are indicated resources; and if our knowledge of them is
only indirect, they are inferred resources. Measured resources are based on a dense grid of regularly distributed
drillings, indicated resources are based on an intermediate grid of regularly distributed drillings, and inferred
resources are based on irregularly, sometimes sporadically distributed drillings, where the continuity of ore grades is
mostly supported by concepts on the theoretical continuity of geological events, such as lithology, alteration and
mineralization. Resources that are either measured or indicated, as opposed to inferred, are sometimes together
referred to as demonstrated resources. Resources of all three categories are sometimes referred to, together, as
identified resources.

         A “reserve” is that part of a mineral resource, which, at the time of determination, may be economically
and legally extracted. Reserve estimates are the result of studies that take into account certain technical, economic
and legal factors, which are not considered when estimating mineral resources. Reserve estimates are based on
mineral resource estimates but also reflect beliefs, at the time of determination, regarding the amount of such
resources that can be recovered and sold at prices in excess of the total costs associated with extraction and
processing. Reserve estimates are adjusted as technical, economic and legal circumstances change. Reserves are
typically first determined at the time of planning a full-scale mining project. As a result, reserves are not reported for
certain of our mineral deposits. Reserves may be “proven” or “probable.” Our proven reserves are based on our
measured mineral resources, while our probable reserves are based on our indicated mineral resources, in each case
after undertaking studies regarding certain technical, economic and legal factors.



                                  GLOSSARY OF CERTAIN MINING TERMS

Alteration: Changes in the chemical or mineralogical composition of a rock, generally produced by weathering or
hydrothermal solution.

Assay: The chemical analysis of mineral samples to determine the metal content.

Breccia: A rock composed of broken fragments of minerals or rock cemented together that can be either similar to
or different from the composition of the fragments.

Brownfield exploration: An exploration or development project near or within an existing operation, which can
share infrastructure and management.

Concentration: The process by which crushed and ground ore is separated into metal concentrates and reject
material through processes such as flotation.

Concentrator Plant: A plant where concentration takes place.

Crushing and Grinding: The processes by which ore is broken into small pieces to prepare it for further
processing.

Deposit: A mineralized body that has been physically delineated by sufficient drilling, trenching, and/or
underground work, and found to contain a sufficient average grade of metal or metals to warrant further exploration
and/or development expenditures. Such a deposit does not qualify as a commercially mineable ore body or as
containing reserves or ore, unless final legal, technical and economic factors are resolved.

Development: Activities related to the building of infrastructure and the stripping and opening of mineral deposits,
commencing when economically recoverable reserves can reasonably be estimated to exist and generally continuing
until commercial production begins.


                                                           viii

Diamond Drilling: Diamond drilling is used in the mining industry to probe the contents of known ore deposits and
potential sites. By withdrawing a small diameter core of rock from the ore deposit, geologists can analyze the core
by chemical assay and conduct structural and mineralogical studies of the rock.

Exploration: Activities associated with ascertaining the existence, location, extent or quality of a mineral deposit.

Indicated Resources: Resources about which our knowledge is substantial but less extensive than our knowledge of
measured resources.

Inferred Resources: Resources about which our knowledge is only indirect.

Leaching: The process of extracting a soluble metallic compound from an ore by selectively dissolving it in a
suitable solvent.

Leaching plant: A plant where leaching takes place.

LME: London Metal Exchange.

Measured Resources: Resources about which our knowledge is both extensive and direct.

Mill: A machine used to grind ore to the consistency of powder or (in wet grinding) slurry.

Milling: A treatment process in which ore is ground into a fine powder.

Mine: Mines are the source of mineral-bearing material found near the surface or deep in the ground.

Mineral Deposit or Mineralized Material: A mineralized underground body that has been probed by a sufficient
number of closely-spaced drill holes and/or underground sampling measurements to support an estimate of sufficient
tonnage and ore grade to warrant further exploration or development. Mineral deposits or mineralized materials do
not qualify as commercially minable ore reserves (i.e., probable reserves or proven reserves), as prescribed under
standards of the U.S. Bureau of Mines Circular 831 of 1980, until a final and comprehensive economic, technical,
and legal feasibility study based upon the test results has been concluded.

Mineralization: A deposit of rock containing one or more minerals for which the economics of recovery have not
yet been established.

Ore: A mineral or aggregate of minerals from which metal can be economically mined or extracted.

Ore Grade: The average amount of metal expressed as a percentage or in ounces per metric tonne.

Ore Deposit: Category including all resources and reserves.

Ounces: Unit of weight. A troy ounce equals 31,103 grams or 1.097 avoirdupois ounces.

Oxide Ore: Metalliferous minerals altered by weathering, surface waters, and their conversion, partly or wholly,
into oxides, carbonates, or sulfates.

Porphyry: A variety of igneous rock consisting of large-grained crystals, such as feldspar or quartz, dispersed in a
fine-grained groundmass.

Probable Reserves: Reserves about which our knowledge is substantial but less extensive than our knowledge of
Proven Reserves.

Proven Reserves: Reserves about which our knowledge is both extensive and direct. Quantities of Proven Reserves
are computed from dimensions revealed in outcrops, trenches, workings or drill holes, and grade and quality are
computed from the results of detailed sampling. Sites for inspection, sampling and measurement of Proven Reserves
are spaced so closely together, and the geologic character of the ore is so well defined, that its size, shape, depth and
mineral content are well established.



                                                           ix

Reclamation: The process of restoring mined land to a condition established by applicable law. Reclamation
standards vary widely, but usually address issues of ground and surface water, topsoil, final slope gradients,
overburden and revegetation.

Refining: The purification of crude metallic substances.

Reserves: Ore deposits for which we have established a business development plan.

Resources: Ore deposits for which we have not yet established a business development plan.

Sett: Settlement price.

SHG: Special High Grade.

Skarn: Metamorphic zone developed in the contact area around igneous rock intrusions when carbonate
sedimentary rocks are invaded by large amounts of silicon, aluminum, iron and magnesium. The minerals
commonly present in a skarn include iron oxides, calc-silicates, andradite and grossularite garnet, epidote and
calcite. Many skarns also include ore minerals, several productive deposits of copper or other base metals have been
found in and adjacent to skarns.

Tailings: Finely ground rock from which valuable minerals have been extracted by concentration.

Tonne: A unit of weight. One metric tonne equals 2,204.6 pounds. One short tonne equals 2,000 pounds. Unless
otherwise specified in this document, “tonnes” refers to metric tonnes.

Overview

         We are a diversified Peruvian mining company and a major global producer of zinc, silver and lead. We
began operations in the early 1940s and have consistently ranked among the largest producers of these metals
globally every year from 2006 to 2025, according to Wood Mackenzie and GFMS. We were the second-leading
producer of zinc, first in lead and among the top three producers of silver in Peru up to June 2025, according to
MINEM. We believe that the quality of our ore deposits, the efficiency of our operations and our economies of scale
make us competitive among metal producers worldwide.

         Our operations are divided into five main units that currently consist of five underground mines and two
open pit mines in operation, five operating concentrator plants and one leaching plant extending across the Junín and
Pasco departments in Peru, with San Cristobal - Carahuacra the largest mine accounting for approximately 32.5% of
our 2024 tonnage production of zinc. Our mining units are all located between 170 and 295 kilometers from Lima,
in the Central Andean region, a center of mining activity in Peru for centuries. As of December 31, 2024, our proven
and probable reserves were 46.04 million tonnes and our measured, indicated and inferred resources were 908.2
million tonnes, which represented an average mine life of approximately 22 years at 2024 production levels (in each
case, excluding the Cerro de Pasco Unit and the Óxidos de Pasco Unit, each as defined below). We have been
granted mining concessions totaling approximately 294,000 hectares, of which: (i) 35.9% are currently being
exploited, (ii) 3.8% are being explored, and (iii) approximately 60.3% remain unexploited and unexplored. In
addition to our mining operations, we also own 868.5 hectares of land near the Chancay port that we expect to
develop directly or through potential partnerships.

RISK FACTORS

          You should carefully consider the following risk factors, as well as the other information presented in this
offering memorandum, before buying our notes. The risks and uncertainties described below are not the only ones
that we face. Additional risks and uncertainties that we do not know about or that we currently think are immaterial
may also impair our business operations. Any of the following risks, if they actually occur, could materially and
adversely affect our business, results of operations, prospects and financial condition. In that event, the market
price of the notes could decline, and you could lose all or part of your investment.

Risks Relating to Our Business

Our business is highly dependent on the price of the metals we produce.

         Our financial performance is significantly affected by the commodity prices of the minerals we produce,
particularly the market prices of zinc, silver, lead and, to a lesser extent, copper and gold. Historically, prices of
such metals have been subject to substantial fluctuations and are affected by numerous factors beyond our control,
including international economic and political conditions, levels of supply and demand, the availability and costs of
substitutes, inventory levels maintained by users, actions of participants in the commodities markets and currency
exchange rates. In addition, the market prices of zinc, silver, lead, copper, gold and certain other metals have on
occasion been subject to rapid short-term changes.

          During the last 3-year period ended June 30, 2025, zinc, silver, lead, copper and gold showed average highs
and lows as follows: zinc US$2,364 per tonne, low in 2024 and US$4,371 per tonne, high in 2022; silver US$18.84
per ounce, low in 2022 and US$35.94 per ounce, high in 2025; lead US$1,874 per tonne, low in 2022 and US$2,396
per tonne, high in 2022; copper US$7,530 per tonne, low in 2022 and US$10,237 per tonne, high in 2022; and gold
US$1,665 per ounce, low in 2022 and US$3,352 per ounce, high in 2025. We cannot predict whether metal prices
will rise or fall in the future. Future declines in metal prices, and especially zinc, silver, lead, copper and gold
prices, could have an adverse impact on our results of operations and financial condition, and we might consider
curtailing or modifying certain of our operations.

Changes in the demand for the metals we produce could adversely affect our sales volume and revenues.

          Our revenues depend on the volume of metals we sell, which in turn depends on the level of industrial and
consumer demand for these metals. Demand for these metals is mostly driven by: in the case of zinc, consumption
of galvanized steel for construction and infrastructure, the production of brass and die-casting; in the case of silver,
its general perception as a store of value as well as its uses in industrial processes and products, such as batteries,
bearings, brazing and soldering, catalysts, electronics and photographic material, and its use by direct consumers,
such as for jewelry, silverware and coins; in the case of lead, its uses as energy storage and in certain other products
such as chemicals, ammunition, oxides in glass and ceramics, casting metals and sheet lead; in the case of copper, its
uses in the construction industry, electronic product manufacturing, power generation, transmission and distribution,
and the production of industrial machinery; and in the case of gold, its general perception as a store of value as well
as global economic activity outlook. See “Industry Overview.” An increase in the production of these metals world-
wide or changes in technology, industrial processes or consumer habits, including increased demand for substitute
materials, may decrease the demand for these metals. A fall in demand, resulting from economic slow-downs or
recessions or other factors, could also decrease the volume of metals we sell and therefore materially and adversely
impact our results of operations and financial condition.

Our results and financial condition are affected by global and local market conditions which we do not control
and cannot predict.

          We are subject to the risks arising from adverse changes in domestic and global economic and political
conditions. Our industry is cyclical by nature, fluctuates with economic cycles and is impacted by economic
instability.

         If the global economic condition deteriorates it could have an impact on our business and our financial
condition. Continued global economic weakness may prompt banks to limit or deny lending to us or to our
customers, which could have a material adverse effect on our liquidity, on our operations, on our ability to carry out
our announced capital investment programs and may prompt our customers to slow down or reduce the purchase of


                                                          16

our products. We may experience longer sales cycles, difficulty in collecting sales proceeds, and lower prices for
our products. We cannot provide any assurance that any of these events will not have a material adverse effect on
market conditions, the prices of our securities, our ability to obtain financing, and our results of operations and
financial condition.

We have incurred losses in the past and may incur losses in the future.

         For the year ended December 31, 2023, our net loss was US$10.0 million. Although we had a net profit of
$137.1 million in 2024, we may incur losses in the future and there can be no assurance that we will be able to
operate profitably during future periods. If we are unable to operate profitably during future periods, and are not
successful in obtaining additional financing, we could be forced to cease certain exploration and evaluation
programs and mine development activities as a result of insufficient cash resources, which could adversely affect our
business, financial condition and results of operations.

Our operations and results of operations may be affected by international conflicts and terrorist activities.

         Our business and operations may be adversely affected by political tension, hostility and instability caused
by conflicts around the world. It is not possible to predict the broader or longer-term consequences of this risk as it
could end in the expansion of conflicts into adjacent countries, further sanctions, embargoes, regional instability,
geopolitical shifts and adverse effects on macroeconomic conditions, security conditions, fuel prices, critical mining
commodities, transport issues, currency exchange rates and financial, credit and insurance markets, and others. For
example, on February 24, 2022, Russia launched a large-scale military invasion of Ukraine and since then sustained
conflict and disruption in the region has occurred and is likely to continue. In response, several countries imposed
broad and far-reaching sanctions against Russia, certain Russian persons and certain activities involving Russia or
Russian persons. Regional unrest, terrorist threats and the potential for war may increase market volatility across the
globe. Ongoing international conflicts, including also tensions in the Middle East, and the Israel-Hamas conflict and
concerns about the relationship between China and other countries, including the surrounding Asian countries, also
have the potential to impact supply-chains, transportation routes, commodity prices and overall market stability,
which may potentially have economic effects on our results.

The mining industry is highly competitive.

          We face competition from other mining, processing, trading and industrial companies in Peru and around
the world. Competition principally involves sales, supply and labor prices, contractual terms and conditions,
attracting and retaining qualified personnel and securing the services and supplies we need for our operations. We
cannot assure you that competition will not adversely affect us in the future. For example, lower cost producers of
the metals we mine could be better positioned to manage future volatility through commodity price cycles. In
addition, mines have limited lives and, as a result, we must periodically seek to replace and expand our reserves by
increasing exploration expenses or acquiring new properties. Significant competition exists to acquire mining
concessions, land and related assets.

         Potential changes to international trade regulations and agreements, as well as other political and economic
arrangements (including direct or indirect subsidies) may benefit metal producers or traders operating in countries
other than where our mining operations are currently located or adversely affect the prices we pay for the supplies
we need and our export costs when we engage in international transactions. We cannot assure you that we will be
able to compete on the basis of price or other factors with companies that in the future may benefit from favorable
regulations, trading or other arrangements or that we will be able to maintain the cost of the supplies we require and
our export costs.

Our estimates of reserves and resources may be materially different from mineral quantities we actually recover
and we depend on our ability to replenish ore reserves and resources for our long-term viability.

         There is a degree of uncertainty attributable to the calculation of mineral reserves and resources. Until
reserves are actually mined and processed, the quantity of ore and grades must be considered as estimates only. The
proven and probable ore reserves and resources data included in this offering memorandum follow the information
management guidelines and international definitions established by the JORC, using specialized software, and are
estimates prepared under the general supervision of our geology and planning managers in consultation with
recognized consultant geologists and engineers, acting as competent persons, based on evaluation methods generally


                                                          17

used in the mining industry. This information, however, is not reviewed or audited by independent or external
experts. We may be required in the future to revise our reserves and resources estimates and we cannot assure you
that our reserves and resources conform to geological, metallurgical or other expectations or that the estimated
volume and grade of ore will be recovered. Market prices of our metals, increased production costs, reduced
recovery rates, short-term operating factors, royalty taxes and other factors may render proven and probable reserves
uneconomic to exploit and may result in revisions of reserves data from time to time. Reserves and resources data
are not indicative of future results of operations and are depleted as we mine. We depend on our ability to replenish
our ore reserves for our long-term viability. We use several strategies to replenish and increase our ore reserves,
including exploration, acquisition of mining concessions and investing in technology that could extend the life of a
mine by allowing us to cost-effectively process ore types that were previously considered uneconomic. However,
we cannot assure you that we will be able to continue with our strategy to replenish reserves indefinitely.

Our exploration efforts are highly speculative in nature and may be unsuccessful.

          Mining exploration is highly speculative in nature, involves many risks and is frequently unsuccessful.
Moreover, once mineralization is discovered, it may take a number of years from the initial phases of drilling before
production is possible, during which time the economic feasibility of production may change. Substantial
expenditures are required to establish proven and probable ore reserves through drilling, to determine processes to
extract the metals and, if required, to construct mining and processing facilities and obtaining the rights on the land
and resources required to develop the mining activities. We have approximately 294,000 hectares of mining
concessions, of which 35.9% are currently being exploited, 3.8% are being explored and 60.3% remain unexploited
and unexplored. We cannot assure you that our exploration programs will result in the expansion or replacement of
current production with new proven and probable reserves.

         Development projects have no operating history upon which to base estimates of proven and probable ore
reserves and estimates of future cash operating costs. Estimates are, to a large extent, based upon the interpretation
of geological data obtained from drill holes and other sampling techniques, and feasibility studies that derive
estimates of cash operating costs based upon anticipated tonnage and grades of ore to be mined and processed, the
configuration of the ore body, expected recovery rates of metal from the ore, comparable facility and equipment
operating costs, anticipated climatic conditions and other factors. As a result, actual cash operating costs and
economic returns based upon development of proven and probable ore reserves may differ significantly from those
originally estimated. Moreover, significant decreases in actual or expected prices may mean reserves, once found,
will be uneconomical to mine.

Public health threats could have an adverse effect on the Peruvian economy.

         Peru has been and could in the future be adversely affected by the effects of contagious diseases. As true
for most economic sectors, the Peruvian mining sector was negatively affected by the COVID-19 pandemic both
directly and indirectly, mostly because of public health measures imposed, such as business closings, lockdowns,
and restrictions on travel and gatherings, among others, which negatively impacted mining companies as well as
their customers, counterparties, employees, supply chain and other stakeholders. The exact ramifications of any

Overview

         We are a diversified Peruvian mining company and a major global producer of zinc, silver and lead. We
began operations in the early 1940s and have consistently ranked among the largest producers of these metals
globally every year from 2006 to 2025, according to Wood Mackenzie and GFMS. We were the second-leading
producer of zinc, first in lead and among the top three producers of silver in Peru up to June 2025, according to
MINEM. We believe that the quality of our ore deposits, the efficiency of our operations and our economies of scale
make us competitive among metal producers worldwide.

         Our operations are divided into five main units that currently consist of five underground mines and two
open pit mines in operation, five operating concentrator plants and one leaching plant extending across the Junín and
Pasco departments in Peru, with San Cristobal - Carahuacra the largest mine accounting for approximately 32.5% of
our 2024 tonnage production of zinc. Our mining units are all located between 170 and 295 kilometers from Lima,
in the Central Andean region, a center of mining activity in Peru for centuries. As of December 31, 2024, our proven
and probable reserves were 46.04 million tonnes and our measured, indicated and inferred resources were 908.2
million tonnes, which represented an average mine life of approximately 22 years at 2024 production levels (in each
case, excluding the Cerro de Pasco Unit and the Óxidos de Pasco Unit, each as defined below). We have been
granted mining concessions totaling approximately 294,000 hectares, of which: (i) 35.9% are currently being
exploited, (ii) 3.8% are being explored, and (iii) approximately 60.3% remain unexploited and unexplored. In
addition to our mining operations, we also own 868.5 hectares of land near the Chancay port that we expect to
develop directly or through potential partnerships.

         In the six-month period ended June 30, 2025, we had sales of US$568.0 million, net profit of US$72.5
million and Adjusted EBITDA of US$223.3 million. In the first six months of 2025, zinc represented 51%, silver
represented 33%, lead represented 11%, gold represented 3% and copper represented 3% of our sales by value. For
the year ended December 31, 2024, we had sales of US$960.5 million, net profit of US$137.1 million and Adjusted
EBITDA of US$381.8 million. We had Adjusted EBITDA of US$380.6 million for the year ended December 31,
2021, and US$297.5 million for the year ended December 31, 2022. In 2024, zinc represented 50%, silver
represented 33%, lead represented 10%, gold represented 3% and copper represented 4% of our sales by value. In
2024, concentrator plants treated 8.2 million dry tonnes of ore grading on average, 3.5% zinc, 1.9 silver ounces per
tonne, 1.0% lead and 0.1% copper, and the Oxides leaching plant treated 0.9 million dry tonnes of ore grading 6.3
silver ounces per tonne and 0.5 gold grams per tonne. We are currently developing projects to expand our
production such as Romina, Esperanza and Zoraida. See “Business—Growth Projects.” For a reconciliation of
Adjusted EBITDA to profit for the period/year, see “Selected Consolidated Financial Data.”

Key Factors Affecting Our Business and Results of Operations

          Metal Prices. Our financial performance is significantly affected by the market prices of zinc, lead, silver
and, to a lesser extent, copper. Metal prices have historically been subject to wide fluctuations and are affected by
numerous factors beyond our control. These factors, which affect each metal to varying degrees, include
international economic and political conditions, levels of supply and demand, the availability and cost of substitutes,
inventory levels maintained by producers and others, and, to a lesser degree, inventory carrying costs and currency
exchange rates. In addition, the market prices of certain metals have on occasion been subject to rapid short-term
changes due to speculative activities. .For example, in the first half of 2025, metal prices, except for lead, increased

implemented by China. Furthermore, the tariffs imposed by the Trump administration have positively impacted gold
and silver as safe-haven assets. The following table sets forth the average published market prices for the metals and
periods indicated.

           The key drivers and recent trends of each of the metals that we produce are:

          Zinc is a major component of the construction and automotive industries, mainly due to its galvanizing
           applications. At the beginning of 2025, metal prices remained relatively high, although slightly below the
           levels seen at the end of 2024. In the second quarter of 2025, growing concerns over the trade war initiated
           by President Trump led to a decline in global markets, negatively impacting zinc prices. However, the
           introduction of a stimulus economic package by China, which included interest rate cuts and a significant
           liquidity injection, helped stabilize zinc prices, which have remained relatively steady. As of June 30, 2025,
           the price of zinc was US$2,650.91 per tonne.

          Silver is generally seen as store of value and therefore its price tends to be resilient in times of economic
           uncertainty. In addition, applications in electronics and solar cells have added to the already wide spread
           uses of silver in photography, currency, jewelry and silverware. Due to the weakness of the US dollar and
           the tariffs implemented by the Trump administration throughout the year, silver prices have followed the
           same trend as gold, acting as a safe haven amid the current market uncertainty. In the first half of 2025,
           silver prices increased compared to the average price in the first half 2024 from US$26.1 per ounce to an
           average of US$32.80 per ounce in the first half of 2025. As of June 30, 2025, the price of silver was US$
           35.94 per ounce.

          Lead is used as energy storage and in certain other products such as ammunition, oxides in glass and
           ceramics, casting metals and sheet lead. As in the case of zinc, lead prices have also been guided by the
           growing concerns over the trade disputes between United States and China, and to a lesser extent, by the
           impact of the Chinese economy. Nonetheless, lead’s own demand structure as an energy storing metal has
           resulted in its price diverging from zinc, with lower prices in several periods since late 2015. Opposition to
           lead-related projects has hampered the potential for increased demand for lead amid more battery demand.
           From the end of 2021 to the end of 2024, the price of lead has been on the rise, primarily due to high
           automobile penetration rates in various countries. Additionally, new technologies have spurred fresh
           demand for lead, such as mobile data networks and electronic personal vehicles like electric bicycles.
           During the first half of 2025, however, lead prices experienced a downturn, predominantly attributable to
           the uncertainty caused by the imposed tariffs by the United States government. As of June 30, 2025, the
           price of lead stood at US$1,972.88 per tonne.

          Copper is used for construction, power generation and transmission, electronic product manufacturing, and
           the production of industrial machinery and transportation vehicles. Similar to the other metals described
           above, the price of copper was also initially negatively impacted as a result of the trade disputes between
           the United States and China. However, this decrease was rapidly mitigated by strong economic results from
           China and the further removal of the previously imposed 50% tariff on the metal by the United States
           government, which has resulted in the price remaining stable to date. As of June 30, 2025, the price of
           copper was US$10,040 per tonne.

         Costs and Expenses. Our ability to manage our costs and expenses affects our business performance. We
strongly focus on controlling and limiting our costs and expenses so that we are better prepared to overcome less
favorable pricing conditions. The quality and richness of our ore deposits and our economies of scale allow us to be
one of the lowest cost metal producers worldwide. Our unit cost of production increased by 25.4% in the last five
years, from US$41.3 per metric tonne in the second quarter of 2020 to US$51.8 per metric tonne in the second
quarter of 2025.
         The largest components of our cost structure are contractors’ expenses, production materials and supplies,
labor and energy expenses, which accounted for approximately 44%, 26%, 20% and 11%, respectively, of our
production costs in the first six months of 2025. In 2024, contractors’ expenses accounted for approximately 44%,
production materials and supplies accounted for approximately 27%, labor accounted for approximately 18% and
energy expenses accounted for approximately 11% of our production costs. In the past we have been able to react
quickly to commodity price cycles by reducing controllable costs, such as exploration projects and mining
development, achieving significant cost reductions.
         Our continuous improvement program, Volcan Avanza, focuses on optimizing and standardizing our
internal processes, cost reduction opportunities, and transforming the culture of operational excellence in all of our
mining units. Through Volcan Avanza, during 2024, we focused our efforts on reducing the consumption of supplies
in all mining cycle activities, mechanical and electrical maintenance and use of reagents without disrupting normal
course of business and maintaining global safety standards. Since the implementation of the Volcan Avanza
program in 2022, the company has achieved savings of US$ 28.1 million in 2022, US$ 27.2 million in 2023 and
US$ 33.2 million in 2024. Among other cost saving and productivity initiatives, we suspended operations at Islay
Mine, which has been in suspension since July 2023. We also believe that the Volcan Avanza initiatives allow us to
mitigate many external market effects such as international metal prices, inflation and exchange rates, among others.

          Commercial Terms. The commercial terms that we negotiate for our sales affect our business performance.
We sell our products through long-term contracts and tenders. In 2024, approximately 32% of our sales were under
long-term contracts and 68% under tenders. Our client base is composed of major global commodity traders and
refineries. We have significant negotiating leverage and typically obtain very competitive commercial terms for our
products. Sales prices for our products are established principally by reference to prices quoted on the London Metal
Exchange and London Bullion Market. Pricing is based on prevailing average prices for the relevant metal for a
given period, generally for the month of shipment, the month following the month of shipment or the second month
following the month of shipment. Revenues are recorded at provisional prices determined at the time of shipment.
Usually, an adjustment is then made after delivery of the products, based on the final pricing terms, the final tonnage
delivered (FOB and CIF tonnages are determined at destination) and the final metal contents delivered. Sales to
trading companies accounted for approximately 69% of our sales by value in 2024 and 77% in the first six months
of 2025.

          We take advantage of our leading position in the Central Andes in terms of tonnage and a diversified high
quality product basket. The Central Andes is home to several other major mining operations. As a result, this area is
one of the most important concentrate hubs of the world. In addition, trading companies have a long history in the
region and are generally willing to accept premium terms for our concentrates, as our volume and quality is needed
to offset other producers’ low volume and especially lower quality concentrates. In general, because of the quality
and volume of our production, we have several alternatives to choose from when placing our sales.

         Hedging Operations. We generally use metal commodity futures in order to reduce the risk associated with
metal price volatility. In addition, we may use foreign currency forwards to mitigate the risk related to our
U.S. dollar revenues and certain payments we make in soles. Our hedging policy is approved by our board of
directors and our current approval consist of hedging up to 45% of zinc and silver separately per calendar year. The
net result of hedging operations in the comprehensive income statement was a profit of US$0.719 million in 2024
and a loss of US$9.269 million in the first six months of 2025. Currently, we remain active in hedging operations.
See “Risk Factors—Risks Relating to Our Business—We engage in hedging activity which may not be successful

approved by the board of directors and are generally paid during the fourth quarter of each year, and (ii) final
dividends, which are paid in accordance with the annual shareholders’ meeting. However, the amount and timing of
such payments are subject to the final approval at such annual shareholders’ meeting and board of directors’
meeting, as well as to the availability of earnings to distribute. Peruvian corporations law (law No. 26887, as
amended, Ley General de Sociedades) establishes a mandatory dividend of 50% or less of the previous year’s after-

the total common stock outstanding.

Reserves and Resources

Methodology

        The information on reserves and resources included in this offering memorandum has been prepared
following the reporting guidelines and international definitions established by the JORC. Such information was
prepared under the general supervision of our geology and planning managers.

         The mineral resources listed in this offering memorandum also include those that originate reserves. This
information is not, however, typically subject to review or audit by independent or external experts.

           Mineral resources are veins and ore bodies of economic value that have been identified and evaluated
through exploration, reconnaissance and sampling. Resources are estimated based on geological knowledge about
the deposit, which is based on scientific concepts concerning the formation of minerals such as oxides, sulfides and
mixed ores, as well as available knowledge concerning the geological continuity of the mineralized sectors. This is
based on technical parameters, such as robustness of the genetic-geological model and its validation through
drillings.

          Resources may be subdivided further, based on the degree of knowledge that we have of their extent and
composition. If our knowledge of the resources is extensive and direct, they are measured resources; if our
knowledge of them is substantial but less extensive, they are indicated resources; and if our knowledge of them is
only indirect, they are inferred resources. Measured resources are based on a dense grid of regularly distributed
drillings, indicated resources are based on an intermediate grid of regularly distributed drillings, and inferred
resources are based on irregularly, sometimes sporadically distributed drillings, where the continuity of ore grades is
mostly supported by concepts on the theoretical continuity of geological events, such as lithology, alteration and
mineralization. Resources that are either measured or indicated, as opposed to inferred, are sometimes together
referred to as demonstrated resources. Resources of all three categories are sometimes referred to together as
identified resources.




                                                          69

A “reserve” is that part of a mineral resource, which, at the time of determination, may be economically
and legally extracted. Reserve estimates are the result of studies that take into account certain technical, economic
and legal factors, which are not considered when estimating mineral resources. Reserve estimates are based on
mineral resource estimates but also reflect knowledge, at the time of determination, regarding the amount of such
resources that can be recovered and sold at prices in excess of the total costs associated with extraction and
processing. Reserve estimates are adjusted as technical, economic and legal circumstances change. Reserves are
typically first determined at the time of planning a full-scale mining project. As a result, reserves are not reported for
certain of our mineral deposits. Reserves may be “proven” or “probable.” Our proven reserves are based on our
measured mineral resources, while our probable reserves are based on our indicated mineral resources, in each case
after undertaking studies regarding certain technical, economic and legal factors.

            The drilling programs during 2024 were strategically subdivided as follows: (i) exploration drilling, to
incorporate new economically inferred resources and evaluate areas with high geological-economic potential, and
(ii) infill drilling, aimed at reclassifying inferred resources to indicated and indicated to measured, with the objective
of increasing geological certainty of the mining plan blocks and replenishing and increasing reserves, that is,
dynamically relocating drilling programs in strategic areas where the highest volume of resources that can be
converted into reserves can be obtained. The development of exploration drilling and infill drilling programs
allowed for proper production planning and ensured its long-term sustainability.

         Mineral reserves are the economically mineable portion of a measured and indicated mineral resource
whose mining is viable based on evaluation with various modifying factors. Reserves include material dilution,
contingencies for losses that may occur during mining, and associated costs for mining. Reserves are categorized as
either proven or probable based on their degree of certainty.

Yauli Unit

        General

          The Yauli Unit is located 40 kilometers from the city of La Oroya and 170 kilometers from Lima and is
accessible by road and railway. It is comprised mainly of three underground mines (San Cristobal - Carahuacra,
Andaychagua and Ticlio) producing an aggregate of approximately 2.9 million tonnes per year of ore bearing zinc,
silver, lead and copper. The San Cristobal mine has been recently merged with Carahuacra mine and we have 154
mining concessions registered in our name which are currently in the process of registration as a merged concession


                                                                                       75

“San Cristobal - Carahuacra” before the Public Registries. The ore is treated at two concentrator plants, Victoria and
Andaychagua, with an aggregate processing capacity of 8,900 tonnes of ore per day. In 2024, this unit produced
approximately 159.4 thousand tonnes of zinc, 7.0 million ounces of silver, 24.3 thousand tonnes of lead and 2.6
thousand tonnes of copper, representing approximately 56% of our sales by value. In the first six months of 2025,
this unit produced approximately 80.1 thousand tonnes of zinc, 3.4 million ounces of silver, 13.1 thousand tonnes of
lead, 1.1 thousand tonnes of copper and 2.1 thousand ounces of gold, representing approximately 63% of our sales
by value in the period, as compared to the approximate production of 70.8 thousand tonnes of zinc, 3.0 million
ounces of silver, 10.9 thousand tonnes of lead, 0.8 thousand tonnes of copper and 1.6 thousand ounces of gold in the
first six months of 2024. As of December 31, 2024, our proven and probable reserves were 20.45 million tonnes and
our measured, indicated and inferred resources were 61.1 million tonnes. The estimated mine life of the Yauli Unit
is approximately 11 years at 2024 production levels, taking into account resources from advanced exploration

Transportation and Shipping

         After we extract the ore from our mines, we transport it by truck or, in the case of our Cerro de Pasco
Mining Unit, by belt, to the plants that then will consequently treat the ore and produce the Zinc, Lead and Copper
concentrates, which are our final products. Concentrate’s destinations change and are organized according to a
monthly shipping and delivery program managed by our commercial department. We transport all our concentrates
to warehouses in the Callao port area except for part of the Zinc concentrates that we allocate to the Cajamarquilla
Zinc refinery in Huachipa. We transport our concentrates to both destinations either by truck or railroad, depending
on the availability thereof and the plant where they come from. The Yauli Unit and the Cerro de Pasco Unit can
easily share trucks and railcars. In the case of the Chungar Unit and the Alpamarca Unit, the transportation method
currently used is trucks.

         Regarding our dore bar sales, we use armored trucks for the transportation of the bars from Cerro de Pasco
Mining Unit to the Jorge Chavez Airport in Lima and the bars are then transported by plane to the country of
destination (which in most cases is Switzerland).

        We use the following methods for the sale of our products:

       CIP (Carriage and Insurance Paid to) Warehouse.

        Concentrates are delivered locally and once the trucks enter the warehouse, risk is transferred. Concentrates
        are usually exported afterwards but we do not arrange the process.

       DAP (Delivered at Place) Warehouse

        Concentrates are delivered to a designated place with costs and risk covered until arrival. The buyer then
        manages custom clearance and pays any applicable tariffs. Concentrates are usually exported afterwards
        but we do not arrange the process.

       FOB (Free on Board) Callao port.

        Concentrates are delivered at the warehouse and stored there until the buyer provides a vessel for loading
        and shipping. The risk is transferred when the concentrates cross the ship’s rail during loading. We arrange
        the export paperwork.

       CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight) “Discharge Port.”

        Concentrates are delivered at the warehouse and stored there until we arrange a vessel for loading and
        shipping. The risk is transferred when the concentrates cross the ship’s rail during loading. We arrange the
        export paperwork.

Sales & Marketing

        We sell our products through long-term contracts and tenders. In 2024, approximately 32% of our sales
were under long-term contracts and 68% under tenders. Our ability to produce and deliver significant volumes
makes us a significant supplier to a broad client base composed of major global commodity traders and refineries.
As a result, we have significant negotiating leverage, and we typically obtain very competitive sales conditions
(commercial terms) for our products.

        Sales prices for our products are established principally by reference to prices quoted on the London Metal
Exchange and London Bullion Market. Pricing is based on prevailing average prices for the relevant metal for a
given period, generally for the month of shipment, the month following the month of shipment or the second month


                                                        82

following the month of shipment. Revenues are recorded at provisional prices determined at the time of shipment.
Usually, an adjustment is then made after delivery of the products, based on the final pricing terms, the final tonnage
delivered (in FOB and CIF tonnages are determined at destination) and the final metal contents delivered.

          Sales to trading companies accounted for approximately 69% of our sales by value in 2024 and 77% in the
first six months of 2025. Sells to smelters accounted for approximately 31% of our sales by value in 2024 and 23%
in the first six months of 2025.

          We take advantage of our leading position in the Central Andes in terms of tonnage and a diversified high
quality product basket. The Central Andes is home to several other major mining operations. As a result, this area is
one of the most important concentrate hubs of the world. In addition, trading companies have a long history in the
region and are generally willing to accept premium terms for our concentrates, as our volume and quality is needed
to offset other producers’ low volume and especially lower quality concentrates. In general, because of the quality
and volume of our production, we have several alternatives to choose from when placing our sales.

        Our main agreements in place for the sale of our products are with two Glencore affiliates (Glencore Peru
S.A.C. and Glencore Lima Trading S.A.C.), Mercuria Energy Trading S.A, Trafigura Pte. Ltd, Argor Heraeus SA,
and Nexa Resources Perú S.A.A., owner of the Cajamarquilla refinery in Peru.

         Amortization of development expenses

          Development expenses consist of investments of sums of money incurred by mining companies before
starting the production stage and the legislator has given special treatment to such investments. Article 75 of the
Supreme Decree No. 014-92-EM (“General Mining Law”) allows companies to deduct development expenses in the
year in which they are produced or amortized within a maximum period of three years; however, it does not indicate
that they must be amortized proportionally or linearly. For as long as we have operated in Peru, we have amortized
these expenses in accordance with the indicated law; that is, for the maximum period of three years, without any
other restriction.

         According to the Peruvian national tax authority (Superintendencia Nacional de Aduanas y de
Administración Tributaria, or “SUNAT”), development expenses must be amortized linearly, despite the lack of
specific regulation governing this specific point. The Company and certain of its subsidiaries have had their
amortization schedules challenged by SUNAT.

        Compañía Minera Chungar has obtained a favorable ruling of the Supreme Court in this matter, in which
the Court recognized that its development expenses could be amortized without any restriction other that the
maximum term of 3 years. However, other companies in our economic group still face disputes on this issue. Since



                                                          94

2018, the Company and its subsidiaries have started amortizing development expenses linearly, preventing new
challenges from SUNAT in connection with this matter in the future.

         Losses sustained from transactions with derivative financial instruments that have no hedging purpose

          Pursuant to article 5-A of Supreme Decree No. 179-2004 EF (“Income Tax Law”), a loss derived from
derivative financial instruments can only be considered for tax purposes a deductible loss if it has a hedging purpose.
According to the Income Tax Law, a derivative financial instrument has a hedging purpose if, among others, the
following requirements are met: (i) the asset or liability hedged must be identified, (ii) the risk to be hedged must be
specific; and (iii) the derivative financial instruments must be entered into or subscribed in a publicly recognized
market. The Company, Empresa Administradora Cerro and Compañía Minera Chungar have entered into or
subscribed several derivative financial instruments in the form of a swap in order to cover the risk of the downward
trend in zinc and lead prices. At the time of liquidation of such derivative financial instruments, deductible losses
were generated for tax purposes.

          SUNAT concluded that the Company, Empresa Administradora Cerro and Compañía Minera Chungar did
not submit sufficient documentation to prove the identification of the covered sales and the specific risk, as required
by the Income Tax Law. SUNAT also concluded that the Company, Empresa Administradora Cerro and Compañía
Minera Chungar did not comply with requirement (iii) above because the underlying prices agreed to under the swap
agreements were not published in the London Metal Exchange (LME). For those reasons, SUNAT disqualified the
loss that resulted from those derivative financial instruments as deductible for tax purposes.

        The Company, Empresa Administradora Cerro and Compañía Minera Chungar have challenged these
SUNAT objections before the Administrative Tax Court. As of the date of this offering memorandum, the
Administrative Tax Court has not yet rendered a decision on the matter.

Zinc Industry

Overview

         Zinc is an internationally traded commodity. The London Metal Exchange is recognized as its principal
trading market. Prices generally reflect the worldwide zinc supply and demand balance, but can also be influenced
by the activities of speculative market participants such as investment funds and by fluctuations in currency
exchange rates.

         An important characteristic of zinc is its resistance to corrosion, which makes it a versatile metal.
Additionally, its low melting point, fluidity, non-magnetic propensity, strength and alloying properties have
increased its general demand across various applications. Its capacity as a surface treatment has proved crucial in
protecting steel products against corrosion and improving their durability. The primary end-use applications of zinc
include: construction (zinc is a major additive in galvanized steel), transportation and automobiles, white goods,
industrials goods and equipment. Currently, there are limited low-cost substitutes for zinc in several of these
applications.

Zinc Demand

         Galvanizing is the predominant first-use for zinc, accounting for approximately 60% of global zinc usage in
all forms in 2024. The next largest use of zinc is zinc alloys, accounting for 15% of total demand, followed by usage
in brass production at 9%. 11% of zinc compounds is used in producing oxides and chemicals and a further 4% of
zinc usage involves its conversion into rolled and extruded semi-manufactured products. In both absolute and
percentage terms, galvanizing is forecast to be the fastest growing end-use, with principal applications in the
construction and automotive industries.

          The largest end-use sector for zinc is construction, which, together with publicly-funded infrastructure
activity, accounted for 50% of global end-use zinc consumption in 2024. The second most important end-use sector
is transport, which accounted for 20% of zinc consumption. The infrastructure represented 15% of consumption and
the remainder was used mostly in household appliances.

Silver Industry

Overview

         Silver is one of the eight precious, or noble, metals; the others are gold and the six platinum-group metals.
Silver occurs naturally in its solid metallic state and is commonly associated with deposits of zinc, copper, lead and
gold.

          Silver is distinct from other precious metals in that it is both an industrial and a monetary asset. Silver’s
value is driven by two main factors: first, silver has a number of distinctive physical and chemical properties that
make it an essential and hard-to-substitute component in several industrial applications, and second, in times of
economic uncertainty, silver is viewed as an attractive hedge against inflation and a decrease in value of, among
others, the U.S. dollar.

Silver Demand

         Silver has solid supply and demand fundamentals, with significant demand coming from diverse sectors.
Industrial applications, consumer use and investment are the three main demand drivers. According to J.P. Morgan,
in 2024, industrial, consumer and photography represented 70.4%, 27.0% and 2.6% of silver industrial demand,
respectively.

         According to J.P. Morgan, total global demand for industrial and consumer end-uses, which is in the form
of manufactured end-products, increased by 1.7% in 2024, to 1,202.3 million ounces. This increase was led by the
industrial category, which, according to J.P. Morgan, increased by 7.2% to 701 million ounces in 2024.

rapid population and income growth, surging demand for consumer electronics and promising housing market are
driving its silver demand. According to World Silver Survey, industrial demand for silver in China has risen from
150.9 million ounces in 2010 to 680 million ounces in 2024, an increase of 350.7%, growth led by China

Lead Industry

Overview

         Lead has an estimated abundance of almost one-sixth that of zinc, with which it is commonly geologically
associated. Lead is not found in nature in its native form, but is commonly found in sulfide, oxide and silicate forms.

         The battery sector is the single largest consumer of lead, accounting for approximately 80% of lead demand
in 2024. It can be subdivided into two groups, including:

         SLI (Starting-Lighting-Ignition) batteries currently account for over half of all lead demand. These are
          mainly used in cars and light vehicles.

         Industrial batteries (both stationary and traction) currently consume around one quarter of all lead
          produced. Stationary batteries are principally used in back-up power supply systems for electrical
          equipment and are also used extensively in telecommunications networks. Traction batteries are used for
          motive power in certain equipment such as forklift trucks and motorized wheelchairs.

         The remaining approximately 20% of lead consumed in 2024 was for non-battery applications. Lead has
several other small uses, which have declined over time as the battery sector’s market share has increased, and all
remaining applications for lead are under scrutiny due to environmental concerns. What may prevent any rapid
decline in many uses, however, is the lack of suitable alternatives to lead with, in some cases, the only alternatives
being of even greater toxicity.

Copper Industry

Overview

         Copper is an internationally traded commodity, and its price is largely determined on the major metals
exchanges. Like zinc prices, copper prices generally reflect the worldwide copper supply and demand balance but
can also be influenced by the activities of speculative market participants and by movements in currency exchange
rates.

          Copper is a ductile, corrosion resistant and malleable metal that is an excellent conductor of heat and
electricity and has significant structural capabilities. The primary applications for copper include electronics
applications, electrical conduit, construction and transportation industries, industrial equipment, and consumer
products. While other materials compete with copper for various uses, substitution is modest because of copper’s
unique characteristics.

Copper Demand

         The world’s consumption of copper has increased significantly in the past five years, as large developing
countries enter the global market. Population and industrial growth will continue to be the primary driver of demand
for copper. The rate of industrialization, especially in China and India, has created a high level of copper demand
over the past decade, while metal use in many developing countries remains a fraction of the intensity observed in
developed nations.

       Copper consumption is largely associated with industrial production and tends to follow economic cycles.
Demand for copper products tends to increase during expansion phases, which often leads to price increases.

        Asian refined copper consumption, led by China, has been particularly strong, increasing by a CAGR of
3.7%, compared to a global rate of 2.4% since 2021.

Copper Supply

        While the earth’s crust contains an almost inexhaustible supply of copper, most of it cannot be extracted
economically utilizing existing technologies. Worldwide copper supply is driven by production rates at copper
mines around the globe, as well as a small amount of scrap metal that is available for reuse. According to Wood
